introduction-what-is-a-process-really.core: A process is a running program: an address space (code, data, heap, stack, mapped libraries), one or more threads (each with registers and a stack), open file descriptors, credentials (UID, GID, capabilities), signal handlers, resource limits, cgroup membership and namespaces, all tracked in the kernel's task_struct. Linux threads are tasks that share an address space, and /proc/<pid> exposes nearly all of it.

first_principles.problem: An engineer confuses PIDs, threads and processes and can't explain why one 'process' shows 200 entries in top -H.

analogy.title: A workshop with workers
analogy.story: The workshop (process) holds tools and materials; workers (threads) share them and each has their own task list.
analogy.breaks: Workshops are physical; threads switch in microseconds.

code.text:
pid=$(pgrep -o java)
grep -E 'Name|State|PPid|Threads|VmRSS|Uid' /proc/$pid/status
ls /proc/$pid/task | wc -l     # threads
ps -L -o pid,lwp,stat,comm -p $pid | head

check.a: As tasks created with clone() that share the same address space (and other resources) with their thread group.

the-lifecycle-part-1-birth-by-cloning-fo.core: New processes are created by fork() (or clone/vfork). The child is a near-copy of the parent: same code, memory contents, open FDs and environment, but a new PID. Memory isn't actually copied; copy-on-write marks pages read-only and shares them until either side writes, so fork is fast even for large processes. fork returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent.

first_principles.problem: A 30 GB Redis forking for a snapshot triggers memory spikes during heavy writes.

analogy.title: Photocopying a book lazily
analogy.story: You both share the original until someone wants to write in it; only then is that page photocopied.
analogy.breaks: Photocopies are instant to see; COW copies happen silently on page faults.

code.text:
# Redis BGSAVE forks; during heavy writes, modified pages get copied
redis-cli INFO persistence | grep -E 'rdb_last_cow_size|rdb_bgsave_in_progress'
# rdb_last_cow_size:3221225472  (3 GB copied due to writes)

check.q: Why is fork() fast even for processes using gigabytes of memory?
check.a: Copy-on-write shares pages between parent and child, copying a page only when one of them writes to it.

the-lifecycle-part-2-transformation-exec.core: exec (execve) replaces the current process's program with a new one: the kernel loads the new binary, sets up a fresh address space, stack, arguments and environment, and keeps the PID, open FDs (unless close-on-exec), cwd, credentials (adjusted by setuid) and limits. The shell's fork-then-exec pattern creates a child and transforms it into the command. Any FD without O_CLOEXEC leaks into the new program.

first_principles.problem: A spawned helper process inherits the parent's database connection socket because the FD lacked CLOEXEC.
derivation: exec keeps **PID, FDs, cwd, env (if passed)**.

analogy.title: A theatre changing the play but keeping the stage
analogy.story: The actors, script and set change completely, but the venue address and some props in the wings stay.
analogy.breaks: Theatres clear props deliberately; FDs remain unless CLOEXEC.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Helper no longer holds parent's sockets.

code.text:
pid=$(pgrep -f helper)
ls -l /proc/$pid/fd     # socket:[...] inherited from parent!
# fix in code: open(..., O_CLOEXEC); socket(..., SOCK_CLOEXEC)
strace -f -e trace=execve -o /tmp/ex.txt ./parent && grep execve /tmp/ex.txt

check.q: Which file descriptors survive an exec?
check.a: All open FDs except those marked close-on-exec (O_CLOEXEC / FD_CLOEXEC).

the-lifecycle-part-3-death-and-reporting.core: When a process calls exit (or returns from main or is killed), the kernel releases its memory and FDs but keeps a small entry with the exit status until the parent collects it via wait() or waitpid(). The parent gets SIGCHLD. If the parent never waits, the child lingers as a zombie. If the parent dies first, the child is reparented to PID 1 (or a subreaper), which must reap it. Exit codes convey success (0) or failure (1–255; 128+N means killed by signal N).

first_principles.problem: A container shows hundreds of defunct processes because its app spawns children but never waits.

analogy.title: A departing employee's exit form
analogy.story: They leave, but their exit form waits on the manager's desk until signed; unsigned forms pile up.
analogy.breaks: Forms take no resources; zombies hold PIDs.

code.text:
sleep 100 & pid=$!; kill -TERM $pid; wait $pid; echo $?    # 143 = 128 + 15 (SIGTERM)
false; echo $?                                                 # 1
nonexistent-cmd; echo $?                                       # 127

check.q: What does an exit code of 137 indicate?
check.a: The process was killed by signal 9 (SIGKILL), since 128 + 9 = 137, often by the OOM killer.

process-states-running-and-sleeping.core: ps shows each task's state. R (running or runnable, on CPU or in the run queue), S (interruptible sleep, waiting for an event like I/O completion or a timer, and wakeable by signals), D (uninterruptible sleep), T (stopped), t (traced), Z (zombie) and I (idle kernel threads). Most processes are mostly S. Many R tasks mean CPU contention; many D tasks mean I/O or kernel waits.

first_principles.problem: An engineer sees 'S' for a busy web server and assumes it's hung.
truths: Counts of R and D reveal bottlenecks.
derivation: Count states with **ps -eo stat | sort | uniq -c**.

analogy.title: Restaurant staff states
analogy.story: Cooking (R), waiting for an order (S), stuck waiting for a delivery that can't be interrupted (D).
analogy.breaks: Staff can multitask; a task has one state at a time.

code.text:
ps -eo stat= | cut -c1 | sort | uniq -c
#  3 D   240 S   5 R   2 Z
ps -eo pid,stat,wchan:20,comm | awk '$2 ~ /^D/'    # what D tasks wait on

check.q: What does a process in state S mean?
check.a: It's in interruptible sleep, waiting for an event (I/O, timer, lock), which is normal for idle or I/O-bound processes.

process-states-the-deep-sleep-d-state.core: D state (uninterruptible sleep) means a task is waiting inside the kernel for something that can't be safely interrupted, usually disk or NFS I/O, page faults on slow storage, or certain driver operations. Signals, even SIGKILL, aren't processed until the wait ends. Many D-state tasks point to storage problems (a hung NFS server, failing disk, saturated I/O) and they inflate load average. hung_task warnings appear after 120 s.

first_principles.problem: kill -9 doesn't remove a process stuck on an unreachable NFS mount.
truths: Some kernel waits can't be interrupted.
Signals wait until the sleep ends.
derivation: Identify D tasks with **ps STAT D**.
Use **soft/intr NFS** options or fix backend.

analogy.title: A person in the middle of a surgery
analogy.story: You can't call them away until the operation step finishes, no matter how urgent.
analogy.breaks: Surgeries end eventually; a dead NFS server may never return.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: NFS RPC wait identified; fix the server/mount.

code.text:
ps -eo pid,stat,wchan:32,comm | awk '$2 ~ /D/'
# 4123 D rpc_wait_bit_killable  rsync
cat /proc/4123/stack | head
dmesg | grep -i 'blocked for more than'

check.q: Why doesn't SIGKILL immediately terminate a process in D state?
check.a: The process is in an uninterruptible kernel wait; signals are only acted on after the wait completes.

process-states-the-zombie-z.core: A zombie (Z, 'defunct') has exited but hasn't been reaped: its memory and FDs are freed, but its PID and exit status remain in the process table. Zombies use no CPU or memory beyond the entry, but they consume PIDs, and thousands can exhaust pid_max or a cgroup's pids.max. You can't kill a zombie, since it's already dead. Make its parent call wait, or kill the parent so PID 1 adopts and reaps it. In containers, use an init like tini.

first_principles.problem: A container's app spawns shell helpers and never reaps them, eventually hitting pids.max.
truths: Only the parent's wait clears them.
derivation: Fix **parent to wait()** or handle SIGCHLD.

analogy.title: A ghost on the staff list
analogy.story: The person left long ago but their name stays on the roster until the manager files the paperwork.
analogy.breaks: Ghost names are harmless; too many zombies exhaust PIDs.

code.text:
ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,comm | awk '$3 ~ /Z/' | head
# 9012 4001 Z sh <defunct>
ps -o pid,comm -p 4001          # parent: app
docker run --init myapp:1.0    # tini reaps zombies as PID 1

check.q: Why can't you kill a zombie process?
check.a: It has already exited; only its parent calling wait (or its reparenting to an init that reaps) removes it.

signals-communicating-with-processes.core: Signals are the kernel's way to notify processes asynchronously. Each has a default action (terminate, ignore, core dump, stop or continue) that processes may override with handlers, except SIGKILL and SIGSTOP. They're sent via kill(), raised by the kernel (SIGSEGV on bad memory, SIGPIPE on a broken pipe, SIGCHLD on child exit) or by terminals (Ctrl-C SIGINT, Ctrl-Z SIGTSTP). Masks block delivery, and pending signals of the same type coalesce.

first_principles.problem: A service ignores SIGTERM from Kubernetes and gets SIGKILLed after 30 seconds, dropping requests.

analogy.title: Different alarms in a building
analogy.story: Fire alarm means leave (TERM), the master key opens any door (KILL), and the intercom says reload the schedule (HUP).
analogy.breaks: People can ignore alarms; KILL can't be ignored at all.

code.text:
grep -E 'Sig(Cgt|Blk|Ign)' /proc/$(pgrep -o app)/status
# SigCgt: 0000000000004000 → bit 15 (SIGTERM) caught? decode:
printf '%d\n' 0x4000   # 16384 = 1<<14 → signal 15 caught
kill -l

check.q: Which two signals cannot be caught, blocked or ignored?

the-polite-signals-sigterm-and-sighup.core: SIGTERM (15) is the standard request to terminate gracefully, sent by kill, systemctl stop, docker stop and Kubernetes pod termination. Apps should stop accepting work, finish in-flight requests, flush, close connections and exit within the grace period. SIGHUP (1) originally meant the terminal hung up; daemons conventionally treat it as 'reload configuration' or reopen logs. In containers, PID 1 ignores signals without handlers, so an app running as PID 1 must handle them (or use an init).

first_principles.problem: A containerised Node app running as PID 1 doesn't exit on docker stop and is killed after 10 s.
derivation: Use **exec form** in Dockerfiles (no shell wrapper).

analogy.title: Closing time announcement vs schedule change
analogy.story: 'We're closing in 10 minutes, please finish up' (TERM); 'new menu from now' (HUP).
analogy.breaks: Customers can be persuaded; apps must implement handlers.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Clean shutdowns; zero dropped requests on deploy.

check.q: Why might a containerised app ignore SIGTERM when run as PID 1?
check.a: The kernel doesn't apply default terminate actions to PID 1 in its namespace; without an explicit handler the signal is ignored.

the-nuclear-option-sigkill.core: SIGKILL (9) terminates a process immediately. It can't be caught, blocked or ignored, so no cleanup runs: buffers aren't flushed, temp files and locks remain, transactions are cut mid-write, and child processes may be orphaned. The kernel's OOM killer, Kubernetes after the grace period, and systemd's final stop step all use it. It's appropriate only after SIGTERM fails, and it doesn't work on D-state processes until their kernel wait ends.

first_principles.problem: Routine use of kill -9 leaves stale lock files that prevent the service from restarting.

analogy.title: Cutting the power to a machine
analogy.story: It stops instantly, but whatever was half-done stays half-done.
analogy.breaks: Machines may restart safely; software needs crash-safe design to recover.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Graceful first, forceful only if needed.

code.text:
[Service]
KillSignal=SIGTERM
TimeoutStopSec=30
SendSIGKILL=yes        # only after 30 s
KillMode=mixed         # TERM to main, KILL to remaining group

check.q: What happens to a process's in-memory buffered writes when it receives SIGKILL?
check.a: They're lost, since no handlers run to flush them before the process is destroyed.

understanding-load-average.core: Load average (1, 5 and 15-minute exponentially damped averages) on Linux counts tasks that are runnable (R) plus those in uninterruptible sleep (D). It isn't a CPU percentage. Compare it to the number of CPUs: load 8 on an 8-core box means full use on average, and on 2 cores it means queueing. Because D-state tasks count, high load with idle CPUs often means I/O or NFS problems. PSI gives clearer pressure metrics.

first_principles.problem: Load average is 40 on a 16-core server, yet CPU usage is only 20%.
truths: It must be compared to core count.
D tasks inflate load without CPU use.

analogy.title: A queue at a bank including people waiting for a manager's signature
analogy.story: The line looks long, but many aren't waiting for tellers; they're stuck on something else.
analogy.breaks: Bank queues are visible; load is a smoothed number.

code.text:
uptime ; nproc
# load average: 40.1, 38.7, 30.2   nproc 16
mpstat 1 1 | tail -1       # %idle 78, %iowait 15
ps -eo stat | grep -c '^D'  # 34 → I/O-blocked tasks drive load

check.q: Why can Linux load average be high while CPUs are mostly idle?
check.a: Load includes tasks in uninterruptible sleep (D), often waiting on I/O or NFS, which don't use CPU.
